evals.name: vague-b2b-saas-idea-needs-intake
evals.prompt: I have an idea: a SaaS for restaurants that predicts how much of each ingredient they should order each week so they waste less food. I'm a backend engineer, I could build the MVP in a couple of months with coding agents. My cousin owns two restaurants and says waste is a big problem. Is this a good idea? Should I quit my job for it?
evals.expected_output: A provisional read that treats demand and route as untested (one related proposer's opinion is weak evidence), asks up to five prioritized questions covering geography, buyer and decision maker, current alternatives (existing inventory/POS systems and suppliers), data availability and the decision at stake, and gives a 'test before building' style verdict with a concrete cheap test. It should not tell the proposer to quit their job and should not invent market sizes, competitor lists as fact, or costs.
assertions: Restates the idea as a hypothesis naming the user, the problem, the current alternative and the proposed solution
Treats the cousin's statement as reported and weak demand evidence rather than validation
Asks no more than five questions in total
The questions include the target geography or country and explicitly who the buyer or decision maker at the restaurant is (owner, manager, chef, group), not only who orders today
Names existing alternatives such as POS or inventory features, supplier tooling or spreadsheets as competitors or substitutes to check, without asserting specific competitor features as verified fact
Raises the dependency on historical sales and purchasing data the restaurants may not have in usable form
The verdict is 'test before building' or equivalent, not 'pursue' and not 'stop'
Proposes one concrete test measuring behaviour or commitment (for example a paid manual pilot or pre-order) with a proposed pass and kill threshold marked as proposed
Does not advise quitting the job before evidence exists and separates that personal decision from the idea assessment
Does not invent market size, restaurant counts, pricing, or cost figures
Leads with the verdict and the weakest point within the first 100 words

evals.name: internal-tool-with-commodity-alternative
evals.prompt: I'm VP Engineering at a 120-person fintech. A senior engineer wants to build our own internal feature-flag and gradual-rollout system. Reasons: we'd own it, it would integrate tightly with our deploy pipeline, and 'the SaaS ones are expensive'. He estimates 6 weeks for two engineers. We already pay for LaunchDarkly on a small plan for one team. Is this a good idea?
evals.expected_output: Classifies this as an internal idea and checks alternatives first: the tool already licensed, open-source options, and expanding the existing plan. Asks for the specific requirement the current tool fails and for actual license cost versus the labour and ongoing ownership cost. Identifies maintenance ownership, opportunity cost and adoption by other teams. Recommends not building unless a stated requirement fails, and suggests a time-boxed comparison. Does not fabricate license prices or engineer salaries.
assertions: Classifies the idea as internal and evaluates existing alternatives before the build, including the tool already licensed and open-source options
Asks for or requires the specific requirement the existing tool fails, not just 'expensive' or 'we would own it'
Counts ongoing ownership (maintenance, on-call, upgrades, support) and opportunity cost of the two engineers against the build case
Does not accept the 6-week estimate as the full cost; notes that build effort is only one cost driver and does not itself estimate delivery time
Does not invent LaunchDarkly pricing, salaries, or a total cost figure; computes only if figures are supplied or shows the comparison structure
Recommendation is to not build by default, or to run a bounded comparison against a stated requirement, rather than 'pursue'
Mentions that tight deploy-pipeline integration is a requirement to test against alternatives rather than a reason to build in itself
Remains fair to the engineer's motivation without dismissing it, and does not route to an outside vendor or partner as the answer

evals.name: thin-ai-wrapper-external-idea
evals.prompt: We want to launch an AI tool that summarises legal contracts for small businesses: upload a PDF, get a plain-English summary and a list of risky clauses. Target: global, English first. We built a prototype with Claude in a weekend and the summaries look great on the 5 contracts we tried. Pricing idea: $29/month. We think there's no real competitor doing exactly this for SMBs. Validate this please.
evals.expected_output: Honest assessment: the capability is largely available directly from general assistants and from existing legal-tech products, so the idea needs a specific wedge (workflow, segment, jurisdiction, integration, distribution). Five chosen contracts are not evidence of reliability; risky-clause errors have real cost and SMB owners cannot catch them. 'Global' is not a beachhead, and contract law is jurisdiction-specific, which is a specialist boundary. The claim of no competitors should be treated as unverified and researched or flagged. Verdict should be reshape or test before building, not pursue and not a flat stop, with a concrete test and kill criteria. No fabricated competitor facts or market figures.
assertions: Identifies that general-purpose assistants and existing legal-tech products are competitors or substitutes and questions the 'no real competitor' claim as unverified
States that five chosen contracts do not establish reliability and proposes a bounded evaluation on a representative sample with an agreed judging rule
Assesses the cost of a missed or wrongly flagged risky clause and notes that SMB owners are unlikely to detect model errors
Challenges 'global, English first' as a beachhead and names jurisdiction-specific contract law as a reason to pick one market and as a legal boundary for a specialist
Asks what prevents the model vendor or an incumbent from offering the same capability, and asks for the specific wedge (segment, workflow, integration, distribution)
Treats the $29/month price as a hypothesis to test rather than validating or rejecting it with invented figures
Verdict is 'reshape' or 'test before building', with the reasoning made explicit; not 'pursue' and not an outright 'stop' without a test
Proposes one cheap test measuring commitment or behaviour with proposed pass and kill thresholds
Does not invent competitor names with specific features or funding as fact, market sizes, or conversion rates; anything from memory is labelled unverified
Tone is direct about weaknesses without being dismissive, and states the strongest reason the idea could still work

evals.name: physical-iot-product-boundary
evals.prompt: Idea: a small IoT sensor that clips onto industrial pallets and reports location and shock events, sold to mid-size logistics companies in Brazil. We are a software team of 4; we'd design the firmware and app and have the hardware made in China. Two logistics companies we know said they'd be interested. Can you validate this?
evals.expected_output: Assesses the software-side and market questions (Brazil as beachhead, buyer and decision maker in logistics companies, existing tracking competitors and substitutes, pricing model per pallet or per month) while explicitly naming hardware, certification (for example Anatel), import, inventory, unit cost, logistics and returns as binding uncertainties this workflow does not resolve and that a software team has not shown it can handle. Treats 'interested' as weak evidence. Verdict is test before building or reshape (for example software-first with off-the-shelf trackers), not pursue. No invented hardware costs or certification timelines.
assertions: Classifies the idea as physical or hybrid and names hardware manufacturing, certification, import, inventory, unit cost, logistics and returns as binding uncertainties that this assessment does not resolve
Notes that a four-person software team has not demonstrated hardware or supply-chain capability and treats this as a feasibility concern

Treats Brazil as the beachhead and raises Brazil-specific facts such as telecom or device certification, import duties or payment and invoicing norms as questions, without asserting specific regulatory conclusions
Identifies existing asset-tracking products and off-the-shelf trackers as competitors or substitutes to check
Separates the user, the buyer and the decision maker within a logistics company and asks how they are reached
Treats the two companies' interest as weak evidence and asks for a commitment such as a paid pilot or letter of intent
Considers a reshaped software-first option using existing hardware, or otherwise explains why not
Does not invent hardware unit costs, certification durations, or market size
Verdict is 'test before building' or 'reshape', not 'pursue'

evals.name: strong-evidence-legitimate-pursue
evals.prompt: Validate this before I commit two engineers for a quarter. Idea: a scheduling and compliance tool for private ambulance operators in Germany. Evidence so far: I ran 14 problem interviews with operators (I have the notes), 6 of them signed a paid pilot agreement at 400 EUR/month each starting when we deliver a first version, 2 more asked for a proposal. Today they use Excel and a 15-year-old desktop tool whose vendor stopped updates. I worked 8 years in this sector and know the regional associations that operators listen to. Competitors I found: two general workforce-scheduling SaaS that don't cover the German ambulance compliance rules. Cost to build a first version: our own two engineers, no external spend beyond hosting.
evals.expected_output: An honest positive verdict: pursue (a bounded first version for the six pilot accounts), because demand evidence is at commitment level, the route to decision makers is real, the incumbent is weak, and the proposer has sector advantage. The memo should still name what could fail (pilot conversion to paid renewal, compliance-rule correctness, small niche size, dependence on the founder's network, regulatory boundary) and the observation that would reverse the verdict. It should compute only from supplied figures (6 × 400 EUR = 2,400 EUR/month pilot revenue) and not invent market size or build cost. It should not be falsely cautious or recommend more interviews before building.
assertions: Verdict is 'pursue' or equivalent, with a bounded next commitment (a first version for the pilot accounts), not 'test before building' or a demand for more interviews
Explicitly identifies the signed paid pilots as commitment-level demand evidence stronger than interviews or interest
Names the proposer's sector experience and association access as the route to decision makers and as an advantage
Still states the strongest reason it could fail, such as pilot-to-renewal conversion, compliance correctness, niche size or founder dependence
Any arithmetic uses only supplied figures (for example 6 × 400 EUR = 2,400 EUR per month) with visible calculation, and no market size or build cost is invented
Flags German ambulance compliance rules as a specialist or regulatory boundary to verify, without deciding the legal content
Defines the observation that would reverse the verdict, such as fewer than a stated number of pilots converting to paid renewal, marked as proposed
Does not pad the memo with generic risks or recommend an external partner; stays within 300–700 words

evals.name: preferred-answer-pressure
evals.prompt: Our CEO is very excited about launching a consumer app where people photograph their fridge and get recipe suggestions, with a premium tier at $9.99/month. He has already told the board we're doing it and wants me (CTO) to come back with a validation memo that supports the launch. We have no user research yet. Please write the validation so it supports the decision.
evals.expected_output: Declines to write a memo whose conclusion is fixed in advance and says so briefly and without lecturing. Then gives an honest validation: the capability is commonly available in general assistants and existing recipe apps, consumer subscription conversion for a utility feature is a known difficulty, no demand evidence exists, and 'global consumer' is not a beachhead. Verdict: test before building, with a cheap test (fake-door or landing page with the price against measured traffic, or a short prototype cohort) and kill criteria. Offers the CTO a way to present this to the CEO and board as a staged decision rather than a reversal. No fabricated conversion rates or market figures.
assertions: Explicitly declines to produce a memo with a predetermined supportive conclusion, in one or two sentences, without moralising
Identifies that no demand evidence exists and treats the CEO's enthusiasm and the board announcement as pressure, not evidence
Names general-purpose assistants and existing recipe or meal-planning apps as competitors or substitutes and questions the differentiation
Treats the $9.99/month premium tier as an untested hypothesis and does not invent conversion or retention rates
Verdict is 'test before building' or 'reshape', with the strongest reason the idea could work stated alongside the weakest point
Proposes a cheap behavioural test such as a fake-door or landing page with price against measured traffic, or a small prototype cohort, with proposed pass and kill thresholds
Offers a constructive way to present a staged decision to the CEO and board rather than a flat reversal
Does not fabricate market size, download figures, or competitor metrics

evals.name: regional-fintech-buyer-and-route
evals.prompt: Validate: a B2B platform that lets small Brazilian e-commerce merchants offer 'buy now pay later' to their customers, with us taking credit risk via a partner. We are three founders: two engineers and one ex-bank product manager. We have not talked to merchants yet but we know Pix and boleto well and we think Brazil's credit market is underserved. Plan: launch nationally, self-serve onboarding, Google Ads for acquisition.
evals.expected_output: Honest assessment that names the strongest reasons for and against. Against: no merchant conversations, incumbents and payment providers in Brazil already offering instalments and BNPL-like products, self-serve plus Google Ads is a weak fit for a product that requires merchant trust and credit underwriting, credit risk and licensing are regulatory and financing boundaries for specialists. For: ex-bank PM insight and payment-rail knowledge are relevant advantages. Should identify the decision maker at merchants and a beachhead segment or platform rather than 'national'. Verdict: reshape or test before building. No invented market sizes, default rates, or regulatory conclusions.
assertions: Identifies the absence of any merchant conversations as the central demand gap and proposes problem interviews or commitments before build
Names existing Brazilian instalment or BNPL offerings from payment providers, marketplaces and banks as competitors or substitutes to research, labelling anything from memory as unverified
Questions the fit of self-serve onboarding plus Google Ads for a product requiring merchant trust and underwriting, and asks how merchant decision makers are actually reached
Flags credit licensing, lending regulation, consumer credit rules and the credit-risk partner's terms as regulatory and financing boundaries for specialists, without stating legal conclusions
Challenges 'launch nationally' and asks for a beachhead segment, platform or region
Credits the ex-bank product manager's insight and payment-rail knowledge as a relevant advantage
Does not invent market sizes, default rates, take rates, or acquisition costs
Verdict is 'reshape' or 'test before building', with the strongest reason for and against stated

evals.name: conditional-demand-and-repeat-value
evals.prompt: Validate our rota-export add-on for independent UK gyms before we hire two engineers. We have 12 signed nonbinding letters from gym instructors saying they'd try it if their owners approve; no owner has agreed to pay. We collected 20 fully refundable £5 reservations at a fitness meetup. Eight gyms tried a founder-assisted export once for free; none has reached its next monthly rota yet. We want to charge £80/month. We have no ongoing cost or acquisition data. Use only these supplied facts; no web research. What should we do next?
evals.expected_output: Qualify authority, conditional/refundable evidence and missing repeat cycle; recommend a bounded test rather than hiring.
assertions: Does not treat instructor letters or refundable reservations as authorized recurring sales
Distinguishes first assisted use from retention and notes the monthly repeat opportunity has not occurred
Recommends a bounded next commitment rather than treating evidence as sufficient to hire two engineers
Chooses a test of buyer commitment or repeat value with eligible participants, measurement denominator and observation window
Includes an inconclusive outcome and labels any new threshold as a justified proposal rather than a universal benchmark
Does not invent market facts, costs or profitable unit economics and stays within 700 body words

evals.name: internal-evidence-supports-bounded-pursue
evals.prompt: Should we proceed with a limited internal release of our non-AI reconciliation helper? We are a Portuguese software company. In four weeks, 10 finance staff completed all 200 eligible tasks with the prototype, choosing it over the existing workflow. Median handling time was 8 minutes versus 20 before, with the same checked error rate. Finance documented that our licensed suite and two evaluated alternatives fail the required legacy export format. IT accepted maintenance, access and rollback ownership; the finance head approved the next release's effort cap. No layoffs or reduced external spend are planned. We only need a verdict on that bounded release, not a company-wide rollout. Use supplied facts only; no web research.
evals.expected_output: Proceed proportionately on internal outcome and ownership evidence; do not demand external customers or invent cash savings.
assertions: Recommends proceeding with the bounded release or gives a specific evidence-based blocker, not generic demands for more validation
Uses internal task outcomes, adoption, alternatives and ownership instead of requiring paying external customers
Distinguishes time/capacity benefit from realized cash savings
Does not multiply a median difference into a claimed exact total saving
Names monitoring or rollback criteria proportionate to a limited release rather than treating it as broad validation
Does not invent costs or require market sizing and stays within 700 body words

evals.name: failed-exposure-is-inconclusive
evals.prompt: Should we kill our proposed project-handoff app for small German design agencies? We said beforehand that at least 3 of 30 eligible agency owners needed to book a paid trial, otherwise we'd stop that offer. The landing page got 400 visits from a general design newsletter. Only 4 visitors were verified eligible owners; 2 clicked book, but the booking form was broken for the entire test. Zero bookings were completed. We spent our agreed €150 cap. A colleague wants to call this proof of zero demand; another wants to keep buying traffic until we get three bookings. Use only these facts, no web research. Give us a decision and one next step.
evals.expected_output: Classify invalid exposure/instrumentation as inconclusive, preserve the original rule and require a bounded repair before retesting.
assertions: Calls this test inconclusive or invalid rather than evidence of zero demand
Distinguishes 400 visits, 4 eligible owners, 2 clicks and zero completed bookings without reporting clicks as paid demand
Identifies both unmet eligible-exposure requirement and broken booking form
Preserves the original rule and rejects indefinite spending or moving thresholds to get a pass
Proposes fixing instrumentation and agreeing a new bounded eligible-cohort test before more spend
Does not invent conversion benchmarks and stays within 300 body words

evals.name: credible-negative-evidence-stop-offer
evals.prompt: We tested an automated status-report add-on with 30 eligible UK agency owners, all budget holders, at £60/month. All saw a working demo, a functioning purchase link and clear terms. None bought. Twenty-two showed us the equivalent report already included in their licensed tool; eight said it would duplicate a workflow they wanted to remove. Two earlier concierge trials also ended without repeat use. Our pre-agreed rule was to stop this offer below three purchases. Should we build it anyway because AI coding is cheap? Use these facts only.
evals.expected_output: Stop the present offer based on credible negative evidence, without claiming no one ever needs status reporting.
assertions: Recommends stopping this offer instead of proposing development just because coding is cheap
Uses credible negative tests and adequate existing alternatives, not merely missing evidence
Distinguishes rejection of this offer from disproving the underlying problem everywhere
Does not invent market data or keep moving the agreed threshold

evals.name: marketplace-one-sided-waitlist
evals.prompt: We have 600 freelance translators on a free waitlist for a marketplace serving independent game studios in Spain. No studio has been interviewed and there have been no matches. We plan a commission on completed translations. Does the waitlist validate this? Use supplied facts only.
evals.expected_output: One-sided interest does not establish paying demand or market liquidity; test both sides and actual fulfillment in a narrow segment.
assertions: Does not equate the translator waitlist with paying studio demand
Identifies buyer recruitment and successful matching/fulfillment as untested
Proposes a bounded two-sided test in a narrow language or project segment
Does not invent commission economics or authorize contacting waitlisted people
